title: Physics Connections Glossary
description: Physics terminology referenced throughout the multi-sheeted tilings project, covering discrete gauge theories, anyonic systems, topological matter, and toy models for quantum gravity.

gauge-theory.summary: A field theory invariant under local symmetry transformations, where gauge fields are introduced to preserve the symmetry.
gauge-theory.definition:
A field theory invariant under **local symmetry transformations**:

$$\psi(x) \to g(x) \psi(x), \quad g(x) \in G$$

To preserve this symmetry, one introduces a **gauge field** $A_\mu$ transforming inhomogeneously. Examples include electromagnetism ($G = U(1)$), Yang–Mills theories ($G$ = compact Lie group), and lattice gauge theories (discrete analogue).

In the multi-sheeted tiling project: **sheet transitions are discrete gauge fields**. The fiber group $G$ plays the role of the gauge group, and edge labels $\tau(e) \in G$ are the discrete gauge field. Holonomy around vortex loops corresponds to the gauge field's curvature (Wilson loop).

examples.title: Electromagnetism as U(1) Gauge Theory
examples.body: The electromagnetic field arises from requiring invariance under local U(1) phase rotations of the electron wavefunction. The gauge field A_μ is the electromagnetic four-potential.

examples.title: Sheet Transitions as Discrete Gauge Fields
examples.body: In multi-sheeted pentagonal tilings, each directed edge carries a label τ(e) ∈ G encoding which sheet transition occurs. This is precisely a discrete gauge field on the tiling graph, with holonomy around vortex loops playing the role of curvature (Wilson loop).

formulas.description: Local gauge transformation of a field ψ by a group element g(x) that varies from point to point.

variables.g(x): group element of gauge group G at point x

references: Yang, C. N. & Mills, R. L. (1954). Conservation of Isotopic Spin and Isotopic Gauge Invariance. Physical Review, 96(1), 191.
Wilson, K. G. (1974). Confinement of quarks. Physical Review D, 10(8), 2445.

bf-theory.summary: A topological gauge theory with action S = ∫ B ∧ F that forces flat connections, underlying discrete quantum gravity models.
bf-theory.definition:
A **topological gauge theory** with action $S = \int B \wedge F$. The Lagrangian multiplier $B$ forces $F = 0$ (flat connection), reducing the theory to a topological theory of flat $G$-connections — exactly the structure of multi-sheeted covers with discrete connection.

BF theory underlies **discrete quantum gravity models** (BF + constraints = gravity), including spin foams and certain loop quantum gravity formulations.

examples.title: Flat Connection Structure in Multi-Sheeted Covers
examples.body: The multi-sheeted pentagonal tiling carries a discrete flat G-connection: sheet-transition labels on edges satisfy a flatness condition (holonomy around contractible loops is trivial). This is precisely the structure BF theory selects via its equations of motion F = 0.

examples.title: BF Theory as Precursor to Gravity
examples.body: General relativity in 3+1 dimensions can be written as BF theory plus simplicity constraints on the B field. Spin foam models of quantum gravity are discretizations of this BF+constraints formulation.

formulas.description: The BF theory action, where B is a Lagrange multiplier (n-2)-form and F is the curvature 2-form of a gauge connection.

variables.B: Lagrange multiplier (n−2)-form valued in the Lie algebra
variables.F: curvature 2-form of the gauge connection A

formulas.description: Equation of motion from varying B: forces the connection to be flat.

references: Baez, J. C. (1996). Four-Dimensional BF Theory as a Topological Quantum Field Theory. Letters in Mathematical Physics, 38(2), 129–143.
Freidel, L. & Krasnov, K. (1999). Spin foam models and the classical action principle. Advances in Theoretical and Mathematical Physics, 2(6), 1183–1247.

aharonov-bohm-effect.summary: A quantum particle acquires a geometric phase when traversing a loop around confined magnetic flux, even when the local field is zero along the path.
aharonov-bohm-effect.definition:
The phenomenon in which a charged quantum particle acquires a phase $\exp(i \oint A \cdot d\ell)$ when traversing a loop around a region of confined magnetic flux — **even when the local field is zero along the loop**.

Classical analogue in the multi-sheeted tiling setting: gliders or CA patterns acquire a sheet shift when encircling a vortex, even though the "sheet field" is locally trivial outside the vortex. The vortex carries **concentrated holonomy**, analogous to flux confined in a solenoid.

examples.title: Solenoid Experiment
examples.body: An electron beam is split around a solenoid carrying magnetic flux Φ. Even though B=0 outside the solenoid, the two paths acquire a relative phase exp(ieΦ/ℏc), producing an interference shift proportional to the enclosed flux.

examples.title: Sheet Shift Around a Vortex
examples.body: A glider in a multi-sheeted CA tiling that travels a closed loop encircling a vortex returns to its starting position on a different sheet — a discrete combinatorial analogue of the Aharonov–Bohm phase shift.

formulas.description: The Aharonov–Bohm phase acquired by a charged particle traversing a closed loop C around a region of confined flux.

references: Aharonov, Y. & Bohm, D. (1959). Significance of Electromagnetic Potentials in the Quantum Theory. Physical Review, 115(3), 485–491.

anyon.summary: A 2D quasiparticle with fractional exchange statistics interpolating between bosons and fermions, possible only in two spatial dimensions.
anyon.definition:
A **2D quasiparticle with fractional statistics** interpolating between bosons (full exchange phase $1$) and fermions (full exchange phase $-1$). Exchange phase is $e^{i\theta}$ for arbitrary $\theta$ — possible only in 2D, where braids are richer than permutations.

Anyons arise in:
- Fractional quantum Hall systems.
- Topological insulators (some).
- Lattice models with topological order.

The connection to multi-sheeted tilings: the **sheet-transition holonomy** has a fundamentally similar structure to anyonic braiding. Gliders moving around vortices in a CA realize a discrete classical analogue of anyonic statistics.

examples.title: Laughlin Quasiparticles in the Fractional Quantum Hall Effect
examples.body: At filling fraction ν = 1/3, quasiparticle excitations carry charge e/3 and acquire a phase of exp(iπ/3) under exchange — neither bosonic nor fermionic.

examples.title: Glider Braiding in Multi-Sheeted CA
examples.body: Two gliders in a multi-sheeted pentagonal CA that exchange positions (one going around the other) may acquire a sheet-label shift analogous to an anyonic exchange phase.

formulas.description: The anyonic exchange phase, where θ=0 gives bosons, θ=π gives fermions, and intermediate values give anyons.

variables.θ: statistical angle; θ∈(0,π) for abelian anyons

references: Wilczek, F. (1982). Quantum Mechanics of Fractional-Spin Particles. Physical Review Letters, 49(14), 957–959.
Leinaas, J. M. & Myrheim, J. (1977). On the theory of identical particles. Il Nuovo Cimento B, 37(1), 1–23.

braid-statistics.summary: Exchange statistics of 2D particles governed by representations of the braid group, generalizing bosonic and fermionic statistics.
braid-statistics.definition:
**Exchange statistics of 2D particles given by representations of the braid group** $B_n$. For abelian anyons, the representation is 1-dimensional ($e^{i\theta}$). For **non-abelian anyons** (e.g., Majorana, Fibonacci anyons), the representation is higher-dimensional, enabling topological quantum computation.

In 3D, particle exchange is described by the symmetric group $S_n$ (only bosons and fermions). In 2D, the fundamental group of the configuration space is the braid group $B_n$, which is richer and allows fractional and non-abelian statistics.

examples.title: Abelian Anyon Braiding
examples.body: For ν=1/3 Laughlin quasiparticles, braiding one particle around another multiplies the wavefunction by exp(2πi/3). This is a 1-dimensional (abelian) representation of the braid group.

examples.title: Non-Abelian Fibonacci Anyons
examples.body: Fibonacci anyons have a 2-dimensional fusion space for three particles. Braiding operations act as non-commuting unitary matrices on this space, enabling universal quantum computation.

formulas.description: Braid group relation: generators σ_i (swapping particles i and i+1) commute when far apart.

variables.σ_i: braid generator swapping the i-th and (i+1)-th strands

formulas.description: Yang–Baxter (braid) relation: the defining relation of the braid group B_n.

references: Birman, J. S. (1974). Braids, Links, and Mapping Class Groups. Princeton University Press.
Nayak, C. et al. (2008). Non-Abelian anyons and topological quantum computation. Reviews of Modern Physics, 80(3), 1083.

topological-quantum-computation.summary: A fault-tolerant quantum computing scheme using non-abelian anyon braiding as quantum gates, with information encoded in topologically protected degenerate states.
topological-quantum-computation.definition:
A scheme for **fault-tolerant quantum computing** using non-abelian anyon braiding as quantum gates. Information is encoded in topologically degenerate states, immune to local perturbations.

The connection to multi-sheeted tilings: the **sheet-transition holonomy** has a fundamentally similar structure to anyonic braiding. Gliders moving around vortices in a CA realize a discrete classical analogue of anyonic statistics.

The encoding of quantum information in **topologically protected degenerate states**, manipulated by **braiding** non-abelian anyons. Vortices and their holonomies in multi-sheeted tilings are direct combinatorial analogues of the topological structures exploited in this scheme.

examples.title: Fibonacci Anyon Quantum Gates
examples.body: Three Fibonacci anyons span a 2-dimensional Hilbert space. Braiding two of them implements a unitary gate on this space. A sequence of braidings can approximate any single-qubit gate to arbitrary precision.

examples.title: Vortex Holonomy as Topological Gate
examples.body: In a multi-sheeted pentagonal tiling, moving a glider around a vortex implements a sheet permutation. This is a discrete classical analogue of a topological quantum gate.

references: Kitaev, A. (2003). Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons. Annals of Physics, 303(1), 2–30.
Nayak, C. et al. (2008). Non-Abelian anyons and topological quantum computation. Reviews of Modern Physics, 80(3), 1083.

topological-insulator.summary: A material with a bulk insulating gap but topologically protected gapless edge states, characterized by non-trivial topological invariants of the band structure.
topological-insulator.definition:
A material with a **bulk insulating gap** but **topologically protected gapless edge states**. Edge states are immune to backscattering and impurities.

The mathematical structure: vector bundles over the Brillouin zone with non-trivial topological invariants (Chern numbers, $\mathbb{Z}_2$ indices). Closely connected to discrete sheet topology in the multi-sheeted tiling framework.

examples.title: 2D Quantum Spin Hall Insulator
examples.body: HgTe/CdTe quantum wells realize a 2D topological insulator with a Z2 topological invariant. The bulk is gapped, but helical edge states (spin-up moving right, spin-down moving left) are topologically protected.

examples.title: 3D Topological Insulator Bi2Se3
examples.body: Bismuth selenide has a bulk band gap but a single Dirac cone surface state protected by time-reversal symmetry. The surface state cannot be gapped without breaking time-reversal or closing the bulk gap.

formulas.description: The Chern number C, a topological invariant of a 2D band, computed as the integral of the Berry curvature F over the Brillouin zone.

variables.F: Berry curvature of the occupied band

references: Kane, C. L. & Mele, E. J. (2005). Z2 Topological Order and the Quantum Spin Hall Effect. Physical Review Letters, 95(14), 146802.
Hasan, M. Z. & Kane, C. L. (2010). Colloquium: Topological insulators. Reviews of Modern Physics, 82(4), 3045.

spin-network.summary: A graph with edge labels in representations of a Lie group (typically SU(2)), serving as the quantum state-vectors of loop quantum gravity.
spin-network.definition:
A graph with **edge labels** in representations of a Lie group (typically $SU(2)$), serving as the **state-vectors of loop quantum gravity (LQG)**. Vertices carry intertwiners; the labeled graph encodes a quantum geometry.

The pentagon's multi-sheeted adjacency graph with $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$-valued sheet transitions is a **discrete combinatorial cousin** of spin networks: a graph with group-element edge labels carrying geometric information.

examples.title: Simple Spin Network
examples.body: A graph with three edges meeting at a vertex, each edge labeled by a spin-j representation of SU(2). The vertex carries an intertwiner — an SU(2)-invariant tensor in the tensor product of the three representations.

examples.title: Multi-Sheeted Tiling as Combinatorial Spin Network
examples.body: The adjacency graph of a multi-sheeted pentagonal tiling, with Z10-valued sheet-transition labels on edges, is a discrete combinatorial cousin of a spin network. Both are graphs with group-element edge labels encoding geometric information.

references: Penrose, R. (1971). Angular momentum: an approach to combinatorial space-time. In T. Bastin (Ed.), Quantum Theory and Beyond. Cambridge University Press.
Rovelli, C. & Smolin, L. (1995). Spin networks and quantum gravity. Physical Review D, 52(10), 5743.

loop-quantum-gravity.summary: A quantum gravity approach where states are spin network states, dynamics involves spin foam amplitudes, and geometric quantities have discrete spectra.
loop-quantum-gravity.definition:
A quantum gravity approach where states are **spin network states** and dynamics involves spin foam amplitudes. Geometric quantities (areas, volumes) have discrete spectra.

LQG provides much of the conceptual framework for understanding **discrete connections** and **holonomy** in the multi-sheeted tiling project.

examples.title: Discrete Area Spectrum
examples.body: In LQG, the area operator has a discrete spectrum: A = 8πγℓ_P² Σ √(j_i(j_i+1)), where the sum is over edges of a spin network puncturing the surface and j_i are the spin labels.

examples.title: Spin Foam Amplitude
examples.body: The dynamics of LQG is encoded in spin foam amplitudes — sums over 2-complexes with face and edge labels, generalizing the path integral to discrete quantum geometry.

formulas.description: Discrete area spectrum in LQG: area of a surface punctured by spin network edges with spin labels j_i.

variables.j_i: spin label on the i-th puncturing edge

references: Rovelli, C. (2004). Quantum Gravity. Cambridge University Press.
Thiemann, T. (2007). Modern Canonical Quantum General Relativity. Cambridge University Press.

vortex-physics.summary: A topological defect characterized by a winding number, around which a field acquires non-trivial monodromy.
vortex-physics.definition:
A **topological defect with winding number**. Classical examples:

- Vortices in superfluids: phase winds $2\pi$ around a vortex line.
- Magnetic vortices in superconductors.
- Cosmic strings in some cosmological models.

In the combinatorial framework: a vortex is a vertex around which the sheet-transition field has non-trivial monodromy. Same mathematical structure, transposed to discrete geometry.

examples.title: Superfluid Vortex
examples.body: In a superfluid, the order parameter phase θ winds by 2π around a vortex line. The circulation is quantized: ∮ v·dl = nh/m, where n is the winding number.

examples.title: Combinatorial Vortex in Multi-Sheeted Tiling
examples.body: A vertex in a multi-sheeted pentagonal tiling around which the product of sheet-transition labels is non-trivial (not the identity in G) is a combinatorial vortex. The non-trivial holonomy is the discrete analogue of the superfluid phase winding.

formulas.description: Quantization of phase winding around a vortex: the phase θ winds by 2πn for winding number n.

references: Kosterlitz, J. M. & Thouless, D. J. (1973). Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems. Journal of Physics C, 6(7), 1181.
Abrikosov, A. A. (1957). On the Magnetic Properties of Superconductors of the Second Group. Soviet Physics JETP, 5, 1174.

spinor.summary: An object requiring a 4π rotation to return to identity, realizing a representation of Spin(n) that does not descend to SO(n).
spinor.definition:
An object requiring a **$4\pi$ rotation to return to identity** under continuous rotations — i.e., a representation of the universal cover $\text{Spin}(n)$ of $SO(n)$, not of $SO(n)$ itself.

Physical realization: electrons, quarks, neutrinos — all fermions.

Mathematical realization: vectors in a $\text{Spin}(n)$-representation that is not a $SO(n)$-representation (e.g., the fundamental representation of $SU(2)$).

In the multi-sheeted tiling setting: the **spinor-like holonomy** in pentagonal multi-sheeted covers is a discrete combinatorial analogue. A single loop around a vortex returns $-1$ in the right sense; two loops restore identity.

examples.title: Electron Spin
examples.body: An electron's spin state is a spinor: rotating the physical apparatus by 2π multiplies the wavefunction by -1. Only a 4π rotation returns the wavefunction to its original value. This is the defining property of a spin-1/2 particle.

examples.title: Spinor-Like Holonomy in Pentagonal Covers
examples.body: In a 10-sheeted pentagonal cover, a single loop around a vortex may shift the sheet by 5 (half of 10), analogous to the -1 phase of a spinor under 2π rotation. Two loops restore the original sheet, mirroring the 4π periodicity of spinors.

formulas.description: The defining property of a spinor: a 2π rotation gives a sign change, while a 4π rotation restores the original state.

references: Cartan, É. (1938). Leçons sur la théorie des spineurs. Hermann, Paris.
Penrose, R. & Rindler, W. (1984). Spinors and Space-Time, Vol. 1. Cambridge University Press.

quasicrystal.summary: An aperiodic structure with long-range order and forbidden crystallographic symmetries, such as 5-, 8-, 10-, or 12-fold rotational symmetry.
quasicrystal.definition:
An **aperiodic structure** with long-range order and forbidden symmetries — typically 5-, 8-, 10-, or 12-fold rotational symmetry. Discovered by **Dan Shechtman (1984)** in rapidly cooled AlMn alloys — initially controversial, eventually winning the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Quasicrystals show **dense sets of sharp diffraction peaks** indexed by 5- or 6-vector labels (one per dimension of the cut-and-project ambient lattice). The pentagonal multi-sheeted tilings would show diffraction patterns combining Penrose-like quasiperiodic order with sheet-structure modulations.

examples.title: Shechtman's Al86Mn14 Quasicrystal
examples.body: The original quasicrystal: rapidly cooled aluminum-manganese alloy showing sharp electron diffraction peaks with icosahedral symmetry — a symmetry impossible for any periodic crystal.

examples.title: Penrose Tiling as 2D Quasicrystal
examples.body: The Penrose tiling is a 2D quasicrystal: aperiodic, with 5-fold rotational symmetry, and a diffraction pattern with sharp peaks indexed by 5 basis vectors.

references: Shechtman, D. et al. (1984). Metallic Phase with Long-Range Orientational Order and No Translational Symmetry. Physical Review Letters, 53(20), 1951.
Levine, D. & Steinhardt, P. J. (1984). Quasicrystals: A New Class of Ordered Structures. Physical Review Letters, 53(26), 2477.

shechtman-quasicrystal.summary: The original Al₈₆Mn₁₄ icosahedral quasicrystal discovered by Shechtman in 1984, showing sharp Bragg-like diffraction peaks with icosahedral symmetry.
shechtman-quasicrystal.definition: The original Al$_{86}$Mn$_{14}$ icosahedral quasicrystal discovered by Dan Shechtman in 1984. Showed sharp Bragg-like diffraction peaks with **icosahedral symmetry** — impossible for any periodic crystal. This discovery was initially controversial but eventually won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

examples.title: Icosahedral Diffraction Pattern
examples.body: Electron diffraction of Al86Mn14 shows a pattern with 5-fold, 3-fold, and 2-fold axes consistent with icosahedral symmetry (point group m3̄5̄). No periodic crystal can have icosahedral symmetry.

references: Shechtman, D. et al. (1984). Metallic Phase with Long-Range Orientational Order and No Translational Symmetry. Physical Review Letters, 53(20), 1951.

diffraction-pattern.summary: The Fourier transform of a material's density, used as the standard diagnostic for crystalline or quasicrystalline order.
diffraction-pattern.definition:
The **Fourier transform of density** — the standard diagnostic for crystalline / quasicrystalline order. Sharp peaks indicate long-range order; their symmetry reveals underlying structure.

Quasicrystals show **dense sets of sharp diffraction peaks** indexed by 5- or 6-vector labels (one per dimension of the cut-and-project ambient lattice). The pentagonal multi-sheeted tilings would show diffraction patterns combining Penrose-like quasiperiodic order with sheet-structure modulations.

examples.title: Bragg Peaks of a Crystal
examples.body: A periodic crystal produces sharp diffraction peaks at reciprocal lattice vectors G = ha* + kb* + lc*. The pattern has the same point-group symmetry as the crystal.

examples.title: Quasicrystal Diffraction
examples.body: A Penrose tiling's diffraction pattern has sharp peaks indexed by 5 basis vectors e_k = (cos(2πk/5), sin(2πk/5)), k=0,...,4. The peaks are dense in reciprocal space but still sharp, indicating long-range quasiperiodic order.

formulas.description: The diffraction pattern is the Fourier transform of the density ρ(x). Sharp peaks in |ρ̂(k)|² indicate long-range order.

references: Bragg, W. L. (1913). The Diffraction of Short Electromagnetic Waves by a Crystal. Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, 17, 43–57.

bloch-theorem.summary: In periodic potentials, single-particle eigenfunctions take the form of a plane wave times a periodic function, forming the basis of band theory.
bloch-theorem.definition:
In periodic potentials, eigenfunctions of the single-particle Hamiltonian have the form

$$\psi_k(x) = e^{i k \cdot x} u_k(x)$$

with $u_k$ periodic. Basis of **band theory** and the standard semiconductor picture.

Quasicrystals and multi-sheeted tilings, lacking periodicity, **do not satisfy Bloch's theorem** — their spectrum is "exotic" (Cantor-like in some examples). The KPM density of states is the appropriate diagnostic.

examples.title: Electron in a Crystal
examples.body: An electron in a periodic crystal potential V(x+a) = V(x) has eigenstates ψ_k(x) = e^{ikx} u_k(x) where u_k is periodic with the lattice period. The crystal momentum k is a good quantum number.

examples.title: Failure for Quasicrystals
examples.body: A Penrose tiling has no translational symmetry, so Bloch's theorem does not apply. The electronic spectrum is neither a set of bands nor purely discrete — it has a Cantor-set-like structure with zero-measure gaps.

formulas.expression: \psi_k(x) = e^{i k \cdot x} u_k(x), \quad u_k(x+a) = u_k(x)
formulas.description: Bloch's theorem: eigenstates in a periodic potential are plane waves modulated by a lattice-periodic function.

variables.u_k(x): lattice-periodic part of the Bloch state

references: Bloch, F. (1929). Über die Quantenmechanik der Elektronen in Kristallgittern. Zeitschrift für Physik, 52(7–8), 555–600.

mermin-wagner-theorem.summary: In 2D systems at finite temperature, continuous symmetries cannot be spontaneously broken, permitting only quasi-long-range order and topological order.
mermin-wagner-theorem.definition:
In 2D systems at temperature $T > 0$, **continuous symmetries cannot be spontaneously broken**. This forbids long-range crystalline order in 2D classical models with short-range interactions.

But it permits **quasi-long-range order** (algebraic decay of correlations) and **topological order** — exactly the regime where vortex defects, BKT transitions, and quasicrystals live.

examples.title: 2D XY Model
examples.body: The 2D XY model has a continuous U(1) symmetry. By Mermin–Wagner, there is no long-range magnetic order at T>0. Instead, there is a BKT transition between a quasi-ordered phase (algebraic correlations, bound vortex pairs) and a disordered phase (free vortices).

examples.title: 2D Crystal
examples.body: A 2D crystal cannot have true long-range translational order at T>0 (Mermin–Wagner). Instead, it has quasi-long-range order (KTHNY theory) with algebraically decaying positional correlations.

references: Mermin, N. D. & Wagner, H. (1966). Absence of Ferromagnetism or Antiferromagnetism in One- or Two-Dimensional Isotropic Heisenberg Models. Physical Review Letters, 17(22), 1133.
Coleman, S. (1973). There are no Goldstone bosons in two dimensions. Communications in Mathematical Physics, 31(4), 259–264.

geometric-frustration.summary: The inability to satisfy all local constraints simultaneously, arising from geometric incompatibility of local ordering preferences.
geometric-frustration.definition:
The **inability to satisfy all local constraints simultaneously**. Classic examples:

- Antiferromagnetic Ising spins on a triangle: no spin assignment satisfies all 3 antiferromagnetic bonds.
- Pentagonal tilings of $\mathbb{R}^2$: angular deficit makes flat tiling impossible — pentagons cannot meet edge-to-edge around a vertex without leaving a $36°$ gap.
- **Pyrochlore lattice** spins: corner-sharing tetrahedra geometrically frustrate antiferromagnetic ordering.

Frustration in the multi-sheeted framework is **resolved by sheet transitions**: the angular deficit that would frustrate a flat tiling is absorbed into holonomy around vortex defects. The multi-sheeted cover is the **frustration-free** extension of the frustrated planar tiling.

examples.title: Antiferromagnetic Triangle
examples.body: Three Ising spins on a triangle with antiferromagnetic interactions: any assignment of ±1 leaves at least one bond unsatisfied. The ground state is degenerate and the system is frustrated.

examples.title: Pentagonal Angular Deficit
examples.body: Five regular pentagons meeting at a vertex leave a 36° gap (5 × 108° = 540° < 360°). This angular deficit is the geometric frustration of pentagonal tilings, resolved in multi-sheeted covers by distributing the deficit as holonomy.

references: Ramirez, A. P. (1994). Strongly Geometrically Frustrated Magnets. Annual Review of Materials Science, 24(1), 453–480.

pyrochlore-lattice.summary: A lattice of corner-sharing tetrahedra that geometrically frustrates antiferromagnetic interactions, hosting spin liquids, spin ice, and emergent magnetic monopoles.
pyrochlore-lattice.definition:
A lattice of **corner-sharing tetrahedra**, realized in real materials of the form A$_2$B$_2$O$_7$ (pyrochlore oxides). The geometry forces **geometric frustration** of antiferromagnetic interactions: no global spin configuration satisfies all local tetrahedral constraints.

Pyrochlore systems host **spin liquids**, **spin ice**, and emergent **magnetic monopole** excitations — phenomena that parallel the project's themes of topological defects and emergent gauge structure on frustrated geometries.

examples.title: Spin Ice Ho2Ti2O7
examples.body: In holmium titanate, the crystal field forces spins to point along local <111> axes (into or out of each tetrahedron). The ice rules (2-in, 2-out per tetrahedron) are satisfied by a macroscopically degenerate ground state. Excitations are magnetic monopoles connected by Dirac strings.

examples.title: Emergent Gauge Theory
examples.body: The spin ice constraint (2-in, 2-out) is equivalent to a divergence-free condition ∇·B = 0, giving rise to an emergent U(1) gauge theory with photon-like excitations in the spin liquid phase.

references: Castelnovo, C., Moessner, R. & Sondhi, S. L. (2008). Magnetic monopoles in spin ice. Nature, 451(7174), 42–45.
Bramwell, S. T. & Gingras, M. J. P. (2001). Spin Ice State in Frustrated Magnetic Pyrochlore Materials. Science, 294(5546), 1495–1501.

renormalization-group.summary: The mathematical framework for scale-dependent physics, describing how effective theories change under coarse-graining with fixed points corresponding to scale-invariant theories.
renormalization-group.definition:
The **mathematical framework for scale-dependent physics**: how effective theories change under coarse-graining. The RG flow on theory space has fixed points (scale-invariant theories), with critical exponents determined by the linearization at each fixed point.

In the multi-sheeted tiling project: **dimensional flow** is a discrete combinatorial analogue of RG flow. The effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(r)$ varies with the scale $r$ — UV (small $r$) and IR (large $r$) regimes have different geometry, mirroring how couplings flow in continuum RG.

examples.title: Wilson–Fisher Fixed Point
examples.body: The 3D Ising model near its critical temperature is described by the Wilson–Fisher fixed point of the RG flow for a scalar field theory. The critical exponents (ν, η, β, ...) are universal properties of this fixed point.

examples.title: Dimensional Flow in Multi-Sheeted Tilings
examples.body: Near a vortex in a multi-sheeted pentagonal tiling, the effective spectral dimension d_eff(r) varies with scale r: it approaches ~2 at short distances (UV) and ~2 at large distances (IR), with a crossover region. This mirrors the dimensional flow seen in CDT and asymptotic safety.

formulas.description: The RG beta function: describes how coupling constants g_i flow with the energy scale μ.

variables.g_i: coupling constants of the effective theory

references: Wilson, K. G. & Kogut, J. (1974). The renormalization group and the ε expansion. Physics Reports, 12(2), 75–199.
Peskin, M. E. & Schroeder, D. V. (1995). An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory. Addison-Wesley.

asymptotic-safety.summary: A quantum gravity scenario where UV behavior is controlled by a non-Gaussian RG fixed point, predicting spectral dimension flowing from 4 in the IR to 2 in the UV.
asymptotic-safety.definition:
A quantum gravity scenario in which the **UV behavior of gravity is controlled by a non-Gaussian fixed point** of the RG flow. At this fixed point, the theory becomes scale-invariant and finitely many couplings suffice to specify it.

A signature prediction: **spectral dimension $d_{\text{spec}} \to 2$ in the UV**, with a smooth flow to $d_{\text{spec}} = 4$ in the IR. This is structurally identical to the dimensional flow seen in CDT — and, plausibly, in multi-sheeted tilings near vortices.

The convergence of multiple quantum-gravity approaches (CDT, asymptotic safety, LQG, multi-sheeted combinatorics) on a UV spectral dimension of $\sim 2$ is one of the most intriguing recurring patterns in modern discrete-geometry physics.

examples.title: UV Spectral Dimension = 2
examples.body: Functional renormalization group calculations for gravity find a non-Gaussian UV fixed point (the Reuter fixed point) at which the spectral dimension of spacetime flows to d_spec ≈ 2, matching CDT simulations and LQG calculations.

examples.title: Dimensional Flow in Multi-Sheeted Tilings
examples.body: Near vortices in multi-sheeted pentagonal tilings, the effective spectral dimension shows a UV-to-IR flow analogous to the asymptotic safety prediction, providing a combinatorial toy model for this quantum gravity phenomenon.

formulas.description: Spectral dimension computed from the return probability P(T) of a random walk after diffusion time T.

variables.d_spec(T): spectral dimension at diffusion time T
variables.P(T): return probability of a random walk after time T

references: Reuter, M. (1998). Nonperturbative evolution equation for quantum gravity. Physical Review D, 57(2), 971.
Reuter, M. & Saueressig, F. (2012). Quantum Einstein Gravity. New Journal of Physics, 14(5), 055022.

conformal-field-theory.summary: A quantum field theory invariant under conformal (angle-preserving) transformations, with an infinite-dimensional symmetry algebra in 2D and applications to critical phenomena, string theory, and topological phases.
conformal-field-theory.definition:
A **quantum field theory invariant under conformal transformations** (angle-preserving maps). In 2D, the conformal group is infinite-dimensional, giving CFTs an exceptionally rich algebraic structure (Virasoro algebra, primary fields, modular invariance).

CFTs describe:
- **Critical points** of statistical-mechanical systems (universality classes).
- **String worldsheets** (2D CFT on the string's parameter space).
- **Boundary theories** of topological phases (bulk-boundary correspondence).

Connection to the project: at vortices in multi-sheeted tilings, the local geometry is effectively **conical**, and conical singularities are a natural setting for 2D CFT descriptions. The holonomy around vortices acts on field modes like a conformal twist — paralleling **twist operators** in CFT.

examples.title: 2D Ising CFT at Criticality
examples.body: The 2D Ising model at its critical temperature is described by a CFT with central charge c=1/2. Correlation functions decay algebraically with exponents determined by the conformal dimensions of primary fields.

examples.title: Twist Operators and Vortex Holonomy
examples.body: In a 2D CFT on a surface with a conical singularity (deficit angle 2π(1-1/n)), the partition function involves twist operators of conformal dimension h = c/24(n - 1/n). The holonomy around a vortex in a multi-sheeted tiling acts analogously.

formulas.description: The Virasoro algebra: the infinite-dimensional symmetry algebra of 2D CFT, with central charge c.

variables.L_m: Virasoro generator (mode of the stress-energy tensor)

references: Belavin, A. A., Polyakov, A. M. & Zamolodchikov, A. B. (1984). Infinite conformal symmetry in two-dimensional quantum field theory. Nuclear Physics B, 241(2), 333–380.
Di Francesco, P. et al. (1997). Conformal Field Theory. Springer.

penrose-tiling.summary: The canonical aperiodic tiling of the plane with 5-fold rotational symmetry, discovered by Roger Penrose in 1974, using two tile shapes with matching rules that forbid periodic configurations.
penrose-tiling.definition:
The **canonical aperiodic tiling of the plane** with 5-fold rotational symmetry, discovered by Roger Penrose (1974). Uses two tile shapes (kites and darts, or thick and thin rhombs) with matching rules that forbid periodic configurations.

Equivalent constructions:
- **Cut-and-project**: image of a slab of $\mathbb{Z}^5$ through an acceptance window.
- **Substitution**: recursive inflation rule.
- **Matching rules**: local constraints forcing aperiodicity.

The Penrose tiling is a **flat** (single-sheet) realization of pentagonal order, achieved by using two tile shapes. The multi-sheeted pentagon framework offers an **alternative resolution** of the angular deficit: keep a single tile shape, but allow multiple sheets. Comparing the two approaches reveals complementary perspectives on pentagonal aperiodic order.

examples.title: Kite-and-Dart Tiling
examples.body: The Penrose tiling uses two quadrilateral tiles (kite: angles 72°, 72°, 72°, 144°; dart: angles 36°, 72°, 36°, 216°) with arrow matching rules. Any tiling satisfying the rules is aperiodic and has 5-fold statistical symmetry.

examples.title: Cut-and-Project Construction
examples.body: Embed Z^5 in R^5 = R^2 ⊕ R^3. Project the lattice points in a slab (acceptance window in R^3) onto R^2 along the golden-ratio irrational direction. The result is a Penrose tiling.

references: Penrose, R. (1974). The role of aesthetics in pure and applied mathematical research. Bulletin of the Institute of Mathematics and its Applications, 10, 266–271.
de Bruijn, N. G. (1981). Algebraic theory of Penrose's non-periodic tilings of the plane. Indagationes Mathematicae, 84(1), 39–66.
